info.desc: More than any other Fleetwood Mac album, Tusk is born of a particular time and place -- it could only have been created in the aftermath of Rumours, which shattered sales records, which in turn gave the group a blank check for its next album. But if they were falling apart during the making of Rumours, they were officially broken and shattered during the making of Tusk, and that disconnect between bandmembers resulted in a sprawling, incoherent, and utterly brilliant 20-track double album. At the time of its release, it was a flop, never reaching the top of the charts .

podcast.body: Fleetwood Mac was actively recording tracks for their album "Tusk" in the same studio where Warren Zevon was working on "Werewolves of London." This serendipitous circumstance allowed Zevon to recruit Mick Fleetwood and John McVie to play drums and bass on his song, respectively. "Fleetwood Mac was recording tracks for Tusk in the same studio so Zeevon was able to recruit Mick Fleetwood to play drums and John McVee to play bass."

podcast.body: Recorded for over a million dollars, a record sum at the time, "Tusk" was intentionally designed as the opposite of "Rumours," featuring a thorny and experimental sound rather than warm and accessible. Lindsey Buckingham largely dominated the album, aiming to integrate 1970s punk and new wave movements into Fleetwood Mac's music. It reached number four on the album chart but sold only a fraction of "Rumours," and was the only LP of Fleetwood Mac's peak hitmaking period where Christine McVie didn't write either the most or the biggest hits. "They spent more than a million dollars, a record at the time, to record their 1979 double album Tusk."

podcast.body: This 1979 LP generated two more top ten hits for Fleetwood Mac, including the title track. The song "Tusk" was noted as a "truly bizarre track" recorded in Dodger Stadium with the USC Trojan marching band, becoming an improbable top ten hit and affirming the band's imperial status. "However, when their 1979 LP Tusk generated two more top tens, including the song Tusk, a truly bizarre track recorded in Dodger Stadium backed up by the USC Trojan marching band, and it too became an improbable top ten hit."
